summary: MPLS networks stack labels on packets, but not every router in the middle of a network speaks MPLS. This standards-track memo defines two ways to wrap MPLS packets inside ordinary IP or inside GRE tunnels, so MPLS-based applications can cross networks whose core does not support MPLS.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine passing a note through people who cannot read your special code. You put the note inside a normal envelope so they can carry it along, and the person at the end opens it.

questions: how to carry mpls over ip
what ip protocol number is mpls in ip
how to secure an mpls tunnel with ipsec
subtitle: How to carry MPLS packets across plain IP networks by wrapping them in IP or GRE headers.

tldr.problem: MPLS applications use label stacks, but two routers that are adjacent on a label switched path may be separated by an IP network whose routers do not support MPLS.
tldr.mechanism: The top label is replaced with an ordinary IP header (IP protocol number 137) or with an IP header plus a GRE header, so the MPLS packet rides through an IP tunnel and is unwrapped at the far end.
tldr.outcome: MPLS-based applications can run across non-MPLS IP cores. The tunnels give no authentication, integrity or privacy on their own, so the RFC describes optional IPsec protection. RFC 5332 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 4023 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2005. It has been updated by RFC 5332, which readers should check for any changes to this specification. The text of RFC 4023 itself does not say how widely it is deployed.

sections.title: Why Wrap MPLS in IP
sections.content:
In many MPLS applications, packets carry a label stack with more than one label. The top label gets the packet from one Label Switching Router (LSR) to the next LSR on its path. That second router then looks at the label underneath. In effect, the top label works as an encapsulation header for the rest of the packet.

Some other header can replace the top label without losing anything. An IP header or a Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) header can do the job. The result is still an MPLS packet, called MPLS-in-IP or MPLS-in-GRE. Two LSRs can then be neighbours even when an IP network that does not provide MPLS sits between them.

The encapsulating LSR must know the IP address of the decapsulating LSR and that it supports the chosen encapsulation. Manual configuration, a discovery protocol or the application's own setup protocol can supply that knowledge. How it is conveyed is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Some roads in the middle only allow ordinary trucks. So you load your special package into an ordinary truck, drive across, and unload it on the other side.

sections.title: Encapsulation in IP
sections.content:
An MPLS-in-IP message is an IP header (IPv4 or IPv6), followed by the MPLS label stack, followed by the message body. The source and destination addresses of the IP header are those of the encapsulating and decapsulating LSRs.

The IPv4 Protocol Number field or the IPv6 Next Header field is set to 137, which marks an MPLS unicast packet. MPLS multicast packets are not supported by the MPLS-in-IP encapsulation in this specification.

When the tunnel's receive endpoint gets such a packet, it removes the IP header. It then processes the rest as a received MPLS packet whose incoming label is the topmost label of the decapsulated packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer envelope has the sender and receiver addresses on it and a stamp saying 'MPLS inside'. The receiver tears off the envelope and reads the note.

sections.title: Encapsulation in GRE
sections.content:
MPLS-in-GRE puts the MPLS packet inside GRE (RFC 2784). The packet is an IP header, a GRE header, then the MPLS label stack. The GRE protocol type field MUST be the Ethertype for MPLS unicast (0x8847) or multicast (0x8848). The receiving endpoint removes both the IP and GRE headers.

GRE has optional checksum, key and sequence number fields (the last two from RFC 2890). The RFC says these are not very useful here. Native MPLS packets have no checksum or sequence number, and the top MPLS label already does the demultiplexing that a key would do. It adds that the GRE key is sometimes treated as a 32-bit cleartext password, which is an extremely weak form of security.

To keep hardware fast and implementations interoperable, a decapsulator MUST be able to process packets without these optional fields and MAY handle them if present. An encapsulator MUST be able to produce packets without them, and that MUST be its default. It MUST NOT include them unless it knows the decapsulator can process them.
sections.plainLanguage: GRE is a second kind of envelope that has optional extra slots. This RFC says to leave those slots empty by default, so everyone's machines can open the envelope quickly.

sections.title: Common Procedures
sections.content:
Both encapsulations share some rules. The encapsulator, whose address is the IP source, is the tunnel head. The decapsulator, whose address is the IP destination, is the tunnel tail. For IPv6, the procedures of RFC 2473 generally apply.

Fragmentation. If a tunneled packet were fragmented, the tunnel tail would have to reassemble it, which a router may not be able to do at speed. Whether fragmentation is allowed MUST be configurable at the tunnel head, and the default MUST be no fragmentation. With IPv4 the tunnel head MUST set the DF bit. It SHOULD perform Path MTU Discovery and MUST keep a Tunnel MTU for each tunnel. This is the minimum of a configured value and, if known, the discovered Path MTU minus the encapsulation overhead. A packet larger than the Tunnel MTU MUST be discarded.

TTL. The tunnel head MAY copy the TTL from the label stack into the IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit. The tunnel tail MAY copy it back, but only if this does not increase the TTL in the MPLS header.

Differentiated Services. The DS field of the outer header MAY be set from the Behavior Aggregate of the MPLS packet, and read back at the tunnel tail, following RFC 2983 and RFC 3270.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not cut the package into pieces on the way, because the person at the end may not be able to glue it back together. If a package is too big for the truck, it gets thrown away.

sections.title: When to Use Which Encapsulation
sections.content:
The RFC says MPLS-in-IP is the more efficient, and other things being equal it is generally preferable. MPLS-in-GRE is for particular situations.

  • Two routers are already adjacent over a GRE tunnel that exists for some other reason. Using MPLS-in-GRE is then more efficient than MPLS-in-IP wrapped inside GRE.
  • Implementation limits may force it. For example, some hardware can only handle GRE encapsulations in its fastpath.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the plain envelope when you can, because it is lighter. Use the fancier GRE envelope only when a road already requires it.

sections.title: Security and IPsec
sections.content:
The tunnel itself offers no protection. The RFC names three problems. The receiver cannot tell that a packet really came from the tunnel's transmit endpoint. It cannot be sure the packet was not altered. And the contents can be seen in transit. How much this matters depends on the application. IPsec support is defined as OPTIONAL.

If IPsec is implemented, the tunnel head and tail are the endpoints of a Security Association, and IPsec transport mode SHOULD be used. Any control protocol that sets up the tunnels MUST have an authentication mechanism. The tunnel MUST provide authentication and integrity, so implementations MUST support ESP with null encryption. ESP with encryption MAY be supported if confidentiality is needed. Manual keying MUST be supported. If automatic keying is implemented, IKE in main mode with preshared keys MUST be supported. For MPLS-in-GRE, the selectors use IP protocol number 47 for GRE.

The tunnel tail MUST know exactly which labels it has given to IPsec-secured tunnel heads, and MUST NOT give those labels to other neighbours. A packet that arrives without IPsec but carries one of those labels as its top label MUST be discarded.

Without IPsec, some other method must ensure the tail only decapsulates packets that the head sent. Inside one administrative domain, address filtering at the boundaries can do this. Across domains it gets hard, and if only source filtering is done, the decapsulator should validate the source address. The RFC does not require that.
sections.plainLanguage: A plain tunnel is like a clear envelope with no lock. Anyone could slip a fake note in or peek inside. IPsec adds a lock and a signature, so only the real sender can fill it.

layers.label: IP Header
layers.detail: IPv4 or IPv6; protocol or next header is 137
